# Abstract

This gazetteer catalogues 821 prehistoric settlements, pit-house villages, coastal shellmounds and megalithic dolmen centres active across the Korean Peninsula and the Japanese Archipelago between 10000BC and 250BC (covering 617.753 km² across fourteen territorial basins). Synthesising regional archaeological excavation registers, the National Museum of Japanese History radiocarbon compendium (Rekihaku v1,3), Korean cultural heritage databases, and Bayesian demographic chronologies [@Kudo2023JapanC14; @Crema2020Jomon; @Koyama1978Jomon; @Habu2004AncientJomon; @Oh2017KoreaC14; @Barnes2015Archaeology; @Choe2002Mumun], the register encompasses every primary excavated habitation node of the domain. These entries span the massive ditch-enclosed wet-rice agricultural towns of the Korean Mumun Bronze Age led by Daepyeong-ri (1.450 residents) and Songguk-ri (1.200 residents), dense megalithic dolmen complexes in Honam and Ganghwa, northern fortified centres such as Namgyong (550) and Odong (520), and prominent Middle Jomon semi-sedentary pit-house aggregations across central and eastern Honshu led by Sannai-Maruyama (650), Kasori (420), Togariishi (380) and Idojiri (340). Across the 821 catalogued entries, the gazetteer documents longitudinal occupation sequences spanning the Initial Jomon and Chulmun stages through the Mumun and Initial Yayoi horizons. Alongside the 821 catalogued settlements, the regional source ledger records 1.476 excluded duplicate aliases and close-pair entries out of 2.297 total evaluated candidate entities.

# Background

Prehistoric settlement systems across insular and peninsular East Asia evolved along divergent socio-ecological trajectories [@Imamura1996Prehistoric; @Barnes2015Archaeology]. In the Japanese archipelago, the Jomon period was characterized by hunter-gatherer-fisher sedentism anchored by semi-subterranean pit-dwellings, communal storage facilities and substantial shellmiddens [@Habu2004AncientJomon; @Imamura1996Prehistoric].

During the Middle Jomon climatic optimum (c. 3500BC to 2500BC), settlements in the Kanto and Shinano highlands and northern Tohoku expanded into large nucleated base camps [@Habu2004AncientJomon; @Crema2020Jomon]. Sites such as Sannai-Maruyama in Aomori and Togariishi in Nagano featured circular layouts surrounding central plazas, monumental six-pillar wooden structures and intensive chestnut grove management [@Habu2004AncientJomon; @Crema2016Summed]. Following Neoglacial cooling after 2500BC, these upland nucleations fragmented into dispersed, highly mobile riverine and coastal hamlets [@Crema2020Jomon; @Habu2004AncientJomon].

Conversely, the Korean Peninsula experienced a structural transition from low-density Neolithic Chulmun coastal shellmound foraging into nucleated, fortified agricultural communities during the Mumun Bronze Age (c. 1500BC to 300BC) [@Choe2002Mumun; @Oh2017KoreaC14; @Barnes2015Archaeology]. Driven by the adoption of dry-field cereals and irrigated wet-rice farming, Mumun villages established dense clusters of rectangular pit-houses enclosed by defensive perimeter ditches and palisades, accompanied by megalithic capstone dolmen fields that marked emerging lineage hierarchies [@Choe2002Mumun; @Barnes2015Archaeology]. This agricultural settlement model subsequently crossed the Tsushima Strait around 800BC, establishing the first moated wet-rice farming settlements in northern Kyushu and inaugurating the Yayoi period in western Japan [@Crema2021Bayesian; @Silva2015Modelling].

# Methodology

Settlement records were assembled by extracting documented archaeological sites from national excavation inventories, heritage registries, and published radiometric gazetteers across South Korea, North Korea and Japan [@Kudo2023JapanC14; @Oh2017KoreaC14; @Kim2021NeolithicKorea; @Habu2004AncientJomon]. All 821 catalogued entries carry geocoded WGS84 coordinates and assign to one of the fourteen territorial basins.

In the regional source ledger, 1.476 candidate records were excluded as duplicate historical aliases, close-pair excavation trenches situated within 5 km of primary site cores, or isolated lithic find-spots lacking domestic architectural remains [@Kudo2023JapanC14; @Oh2017KoreaC14]. For instance, multiple excavation sectors and satellite pits associated with Sannai-Maruyama and Kasori were consolidated into unified site entries with documented longitudinal demographic spans.

# Testing and Validation

Source ledger reconciliation confirms 821 included settlements and 1.476 excluded candidate entries, accounting for all 2.297 evaluated entities without discrepancy. All 821 settlements possess verified geographic coordinates and chronologically bounded population estimates. Figure \ref{fig:sett-gazetteer} displays the rank-size distribution and the leading prehistoric habitation centres across Korea and Japan.

## Sub-Regional Distribution and Ledger Exclusions

Table \ref{tab:regsum-prehistoric} summarises the distribution of catalogued prehistoric settlements across all fourteen territories alongside their leading centres. Tohoku leads all regions with 184 catalogued sites, followed by Kanto-Shinano (139), Kinki-Setouchi (137), Kyushu-Tsushima (100) and the Han-Geum basin (80). Table \ref{tab:excluded-prehistoric} details the leading 30 of 1.476 excluded candidate entries in the regional source ledger.

## Archaeological Caveats and Taphonomic Preservation

Two spatial factors condition prehistoric settlement analysis in this gazetteer. First, differential post-depositional preservation exerts a major influence on site recovery [@Habu2004AncientJomon; @Kim2021NeolithicKorea]. In eastern Japan, shellmound calcification protects faunal assemblages and human burials, whereas acidic volcanic soils in inland valleys frequently destroy uncarbonized organic remains, making pit-dwelling floors the primary remaining architectural evidence [@Habu2004AncientJomon; @Yoneda2002Radiocarbon].

Second, on the Korean Peninsula, intensive river valley sedimentation and modern agricultural terracing have deeply buried Early and Middle Chulmun riverine settlements under meters of alluvium, whereas elevated Mumun Bronze Age settlements on low hills and river terraces are more readily identified during modern infrastructural surveys [@Choe2002Mumun; @Barnes2015Archaeology]. Consequently, settlement catalogues reflect both prehistoric human demography and the spatial distribution of modern rescue excavations [@Oh2017KoreaC14; @Kudo2023JapanC14].
